The Bluefin gurnard, Chelidonichthys kumu, is a benthic triglid fish distributed across the temperate continental shelves of the Indo-Pacific. Field surveys and growth increment analyses from otolith readings have provided a detailed life history profile for this species. As a benchmark for female maturation, individuals typically attain sexual maturity upon reaching a standard length of 21.2 centimetres [Lp = 21.2 centimetres], an ontogenetic milestone that precedes the onset of gametogenesis. At this point, the corresponding wet weight at puberty has been estimated at 91.6 grams [Wwp = 91.6 grams], derived from length–weight regressions. This metric contrasts sharply with the maximum recorded weight for the species, which approaches 1.5 kilograms [Wwi = 1.5 kilograms] in the largest adults, a mass that reflects the substantial somatic investment required across the extended juvenile phase. Spawning events are relatively infrequent, with reproductively active females producing between 1 and 3 distinct clutches per spawning season, a pattern that suggests a strategy of iteroparous batch spawning typical of many temperate triglids.

Early life stages of Chelidonichthys kumu are characterised by rapid developmental transitions under controlled thermal regimes. Embryonated eggs, which are pelagic and buoyant, undergo chorion rupture and larval eclosion after a brief incubation period of approximately 8 days [ab = approximately 8 days] when maintained at a stable water temperature of 19.3 °C [T = 19.3 °C]. The newly emerged prolarva is extremely altricial, possessing a minute mass at eclosion of just 0.0026 grams [Wwb = 0.0026 grams], a value that underscores the profound physiological shift from yolk-dependent lecithotrophy to the onset of exogenous feeding. This yolk-sac resorption phase is critical, as the larva must successfully capture its first planktonic prey before the endogenous energy reserves are fully depleted. The yolk-sac stage typically persists for a period during which the mouth gape opens and retinal differentiation occurs, enabling visual predation on copepod nauplii and small rotifers. The entire pelagic larval phase is a window of high vulnerability, with mortality rates strongly modulated by prey availability and water temperature.

The asymptotic size framework established for the Bluefin gurnard indicates a maximum standard length of 60 centimetres [Li = 60 centimetres], a value that represents the theoretical upper bound of somatic growth for this species in its natural habitat. This ultimate size is rarely achieved in wild populations due to the combined pressures of natural mortality and fishing exploitation, but it provides a useful comparative benchmark against related triglid species such as Chelidonichthys spinosus. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) averaged 9% [GSI = 9%] for actively spawning females collected during the austral summer at a water temperature of 19.3 °C [T = 19.3 °C].

Longevity estimates for the Bluefin gurnard have been derived from both mark-recapture studies and validated age readings from otolith thin sections. The oldest recorded individuals in New Zealand coastal waters have attained a maximum lifespan of 15 years [am = 15 years] under the prevailing temperature conditions of 19.3 °C [T = 19.3 °C], indicating a relatively slow pace of life compared to more short-lived triglid taxa. This extended lifespan is accompanied by a protracted period of somatic growth, as reflected by the large gap between the size at puberty and the asymptotic length. In practical terms, a fish reaching the full 60 centimetre maximum standard length is an exceptionally old individual that has experienced favourable growth conditions across its entire life history. The combination of delayed reproduction relative to total lifespan and repeated spawning events across multiple years classifies C. kumu as a typical K-selected teleost with moderate fecundity and a reliance on adult survival for population persistence in a variable marine environment.

Comparative analysis within the Triglidae family reveals that Chelidonichthys kumu occupies an intermediate position along the slow–fast life history continuum. While the ultimate wet weight of 1.5 kilograms [Wwi = 1.5 kilograms] aligns well with the typical body size of the genus, the wet weight at puberty of 91.6 grams [Wwp = 91.6 grams] represents a relatively high proportion of the asymptotic mass, indicating that individuals invest considerable time in somatic growth before the first spawning event. The gonadosomatic index was 9% [GSI = 9%] at a temperature of 19.3 °C [T = 19.3 °C]. The standard length at puberty of 21.2 centimetres [Lp = 21.2 centimetres] occurs at roughly one-third of the ultimate length of 60 centimetres [Li = 60 centimetres], a ratio that is common among temperate demersal fishes that experience seasonally pulsed food availability. These life history parameters collectively paint a picture of a cautious, energy-conserving strategist adapted to the moderate but unpredictable productivity of continental shelf ecosystems.
